title: Other Vegetables as Ingredient in Omelet

content.title: About
content.content: Vegetables used in an omelet can include bell pepper, tomato, onion, spinach, mushrooms and other fresh or frozen vegetables. They add bright colour, aroma and extra nutrition, making the omelet more filling and wholesome.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegetable omelets are a classic breakfast in many countries, from France to Japan.
Combining eggs with vegetables increases the bioavailability of some vitamins, such as beta‑carotene from carrots.
Vegetables in an omelet are a quick way to use leftovers, reducing food waste.
Dark leafy greens like spinach are rich in iron and folate.
Adding fresh herbs (parsley, dill) boosts flavour without extra salt.

items.title: Rich source of vitamins
items.content: Vegetables provide vitamin C, vitamin A (beta‑carotene) and B‑vitamins, supporting immunity and vision.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from vegetables improves gut motility and promotes satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytonutrients such as lutein and quercetin help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low‑calorie nutrient boost
items.content: Vegetables add volume to the dish without significantly increasing calories, useful for weight management.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Potassium and magnesium in vegetables help maintain healthy blood pressure.

items.title: Allergy to specific vegetables
items.content: Some individuals may react to tomatoes, peppers or mushrooms; be aware of personal intolerances.

items.title: Potential food toxins
items.content: Certain raw vegetables (e.g., potatoes) contain solanine and should be cooked before adding to an omelet.

items.title: Digestive discomfort from excess raw veg
items.content: Large amounts of raw vegetables can cause gas and bloating.

items.title: Salt control
items.content: Pre‑seasoned vegetable mixes may already contain salt; adjust seasoning accordingly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dice the vegetables into small pieces and lightly sauté in a little oil for 2‑3 minutes until softened. Pour beaten eggs over the veggies, stir gently and cook to the desired doneness. Finish with fresh herbs if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh vegetables in the refrigerator’s crisper drawer, loosely packed in a perforated bag. Frozen vegetables keep up to 12 months in the freezer. Cooked omelet is best eaten within 2‑3 hours; leftovers can be refrigerated for up to 24 hours.
